section.title: The Resurrection Body
section.sectionRationale: Paul now answers the practical objection: with what kind of body will the dead come? Using the picture of a buried seed, he shows that the resurrection body is both continuous with this body and gloriously transformed: sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in weakness, raised in power; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body. The last Adam, a life-giving spirit, gives us His own heavenly image. And at the last trumpet the perishable will be clothed with the imperishable, death will be swallowed up in victory, and the chapter ends not in speculation but in steadfast, hopeful labor.
section.thesis: The resurrection body is this body transformed, sown perishable, dishonored, weak, and natural, but raised imperishable, glorious, powerful, and spiritual; for the last Adam is a life-giving spirit who will refashion us in His heavenly image, so that at the last trumpet death is swallowed up in victory, and therefore we labor for the Lord knowing our work is not in vain.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the seed and the many kinds of bodies; sown perishable, raised imperishable; the last Adam and the man from heaven; and death swallowed up in victory, with the closing call to steadfast labor.

units.label: The seed and the many bodies
units.note: what you sow must first die

verses.text: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of {{soma|body}} will they come?”
You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else.
But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body.
Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another.
There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another.
The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor.
So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable.
It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a {{pneumatikos|spiritual}} {{soma|body}}. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

units.label: The last Adam, the man from heaven
units.note: we will bear the heavenly image

verses.text: So it is written: “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.
The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual.
The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven.
As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven.
And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.

units.label: Death swallowed up in victory
units.note: be steadfast, your labor is not in vain

verses.text: Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.
Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed,
in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.
For the perishable must be clothed with the {{aphtharsia|imperishable}}, and the mortal with immortality.
When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in {{nikos|victory}}.”
“Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?”
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.

soma.gloss: Body. For Paul the body is not a prison to escape but the good creation of God, to be redeemed and raised. The resurrection is precisely of the body, sown one way and raised another, so that the resurrection hope is not the survival of a disembodied soul but the raising and glorifying of the whole person.

pneumatikos.gloss: Spiritual, of or animated by the Spirit. The spiritual body does not mean a body made of spirit or immaterial; it means a body wholly enlivened and governed by the Holy Spirit, no longer subject to decay. Just as the natural body is animated by the ordinary soul-life, the resurrection body is fully animated by God's Spirit.

aphtharsia.gloss: Imperishability, incorruption, immortality. The quality of the resurrection body, which can no longer decay or die. The perishable must be clothed with the imperishable; what was subject to rot and death is remade to last forever, sharing the deathless life of the risen Christ.

nikos.gloss: Victory. The triumphant note on which the chapter ends. Death, the last enemy, is not merely survived but swallowed up in victory, its sting drawn out; and the victory is a gift, given to us by God through our Lord Jesus Christ, not won by our own strength.

basic.context: Paul answers the scoffing question: how can the dead be raised, and what sort of body would they even have? He points to a seed. You bury a bare grain, and God raises it as a living plant, related to the seed yet gloriously different. So it will be with our bodies. This same body is sown perishable, weak, and dishonored, but raised imperishable, powerful, and glorious. Christ, the last Adam, will give us His own heavenly likeness, and at the last trumpet death itself will be swallowed up in victory.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul uses everyday pictures, seeds and harvests, sun and stars, to teach a mystery that cannot be fully seen yet. He works by contrast: perishable and imperishable, dishonor and glory, weakness and power, natural and spiritual, earthly and heavenly. The point is both continuity and transformation. He grounds it in Scripture, quoting Genesis on Adam and Isaiah and Hosea on the defeat of death, and ends with a practical charge.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is soma, body: the resurrection is of the body, not merely the soul. The raised body is pneumatikos, spiritual, meaning fully animated by God's Spirit, not made of vapor. Its quality is aphtharsia, imperishability, no longer able to decay or die. And the chapter climaxes in nikos, victory, death swallowed up and its sting drawn, a victory given to us through our Lord Jesus Christ.
basic.typology: The buried and rising seed pictures death and resurrection. Adam and Christ stand again as two heads: the first man of dust, the last Adam a life-giving spirit and the man from heaven, whose image we will bear. The clothing of the perishable with the imperishable answers the shame first covered in Eden, now swallowed up in the glory of resurrection.
basic.christ: Christ is the last Adam, the man from heaven, and a life-giving spirit. He does not merely receive resurrection life; He gives it. The image of the earthly man that we have borne will give way to the image of the heavenly man, Christ Himself, whom we will resemble. And it is through our Lord Jesus Christ that God gives us the victory over death.
basic.god: God is the one who gives each seed its body as He designs, and who will give us our resurrection bodies. He is the giver of the victory over death through Christ. The chapter shows a God who does not discard His creation but transforms it, clothing the mortal with immortality and defeating the last enemy, so that our labor for Him is never wasted.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2 records the first man Adam becoming a living being, which Paul quotes and caps. Isaiah 25 promises that God will swallow up death forever. Hosea 13 asks where the plagues and sting of death are. Philippians 3 says Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
basic.oneStory: Here the Bible's hope for the body comes into full view. The dust to which Adam returned is not the last word; God raises and glorifies the body in the image of the man from heaven. Death, the ancient enemy, is swallowed up in victory, and the redeemed creation is remade imperishable. The story that began with a body formed from dust ends with that body raised in glory, like Christ's own.

context.literary:
The paragraph opens with two questions from an imagined objector, 'How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?' verse 35, and Paul's first answer is sharp: 'You fool!' verse 36. The rest of the passage is the real answer, and it is built in four movements, each stepping up a ladder. Verses 36 to 41 offer pictures from creation: a seed, the flesh of men, animals, birds and fish, the sun, moon and stars. Verses 42 to 44 give the four antitheses in a single drumbeat, 'sown' and 'raised,' repeated four times, perishable and imperishable, dishonor and glory, weakness and power, natural and spiritual. Verses 45 to 49 bring in Genesis and the two men. Verses 50 to 57 reach the announcement of a mystery and the song of victory.

The rhetoric is worth noticing. The repetitions 'It is sown... it is raised' put the whole passage under the sign of a burial and a harvest. The sentence in verse 44, 'If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body,' is a simple argument from the existence of one to the possibility of the other. Verse 46 states a rule of order, 'not first the spiritual, but the natural, and then the spiritual,' which prevents the Corinthians from claiming they have already arrived.

The song in verses 54 to 55 is poetry stitched from two prophets, and the verse that follows, verse 56, is a brief theological footnote on sin and the law. The paragraph closes with 'Therefore,' verse 58, and brings the long chapter, indeed the whole letter, down to the practical business of work. After a flight above the world, Paul lands on Monday morning.
context.historical:
Paul is answering a question that educated people at Corinth would have found reasonable and even funny. Greek thought could imagine a soul living on, but a raised corpse seemed a revolting idea, and the question 'with what kind of body?' has the tone of a scoff. The question may also be a practical puzzle from believers who had buried loved ones and knew the body decayed.

Paul's replies draw on things anyone could see. Every Corinthian had seen farmers sow seed, and the sight of a bare grain going into the ground and coming up as a green shoot was a yearly miracle. The sun, moon and stars were the brightest things in the ancient sky, and in the Jewish tradition they could stand for the righteous. Daniel 12:3 says that 'the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens.' The kinds of flesh in verse 39 follow the lists of creatures in Genesis 1, which Paul assumes they will recognise.

The trumpet had a long history in Israel as the signal of God's presence and action, at Sinai, in war, and at feasts. The original hearers would have known the trumpet as the sound that gathered the people and announced that something decisive was about to happen.

The words 'those who have fallen asleep' and the statement 'we will not all sleep' show that the early church lived in expectation of the Lord's return and had begun to bury members. The question of what happens to those who die before that day, and to those who are alive on it, is the pastoral setting of verses 51 and 52. Paul does not hide his own sense that the return might come in his lifetime, but he never sets a date.
context.canonical:
Verses 45 and 47 interpret the creation story. 'The first man Adam became a living being' draws on Genesis 2:7, where the LORD God formed man from the dust and breathed life into him. Paul adds the contrast: the last Adam is a life-giving spirit, and in the same breath the man of dust is set against the man from heaven. The idea of being made in the image of God, Genesis 1:26 to 27, is the background of verse 49's talk of bearing a likeness.

The final song joins two Old Testament passages. Isaiah 25:8, 'He will swallow up death forever,' is in the middle of a vision of a feast for all nations in which God wipes away tears. Hosea 13:14, 'Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?' is a cry of defiance in the middle of a prophecy of judgment. Paul takes them both as the promise of the day the seed finally rises.

Other Scriptures fill in the picture. Daniel 12:2 to 3 promises that those who sleep in the dust will awake and the wise will shine like the stars, Isaiah 26:19 says, 'Your dead will live; their bodies will rise,' and Philippians 3:20 to 21 says Christ 'will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.' In 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to 17 the Lord descends 'with the trumpet of God' and the dead in Christ rise first, and Paul's mystery of verse 51 sits alongside it. Romans 8:11 and 8:23 tie the rising to the Spirit and speak of 'the redemption of our bodies,' and 1 John 3:2 says that when Christ appears 'we will be like Him.' Jesus' own word in John 12:24 about the kernel of wheat that falls into the ground is the seed principle in a sentence.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted to answer a scoffing question with something better than an argument. He gives pictures. The seed does not prove the resurrection, but it breaks the objector's assumption that what is buried and what is raised must be identical or else unrelated. God makes a plant from a seed, and He may make a glorious body from a perishable one. The word 'fool' is blunt, but it is the voice of a pastor who has heard a clever objection and wants to bring people back to wonder.

He also wanted to hold two things together that the Corinthians were tempted to separate. On one side, the hope is bodily; the body is not thrown away like a husk. On the other side, the body that rises is no mere resuscitation of what lies in the grave, but a new and glorious form. Both must stand. A faith that loses the first becomes a ghostly spirituality, and one that loses the second imagines heaven as more of the same.

And he meant the passage to end in work. The last verse is not an afterthought. Because the dead will be raised, nothing done for Christ is wasted. A church that has been told its labour is not in vain can bear the weariness of a world in which graves still exist.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is description of what God will do, and only the last verse commands. We are not told how the change will happen, what it will feel like, or what the glorified body will be able to do. Paul uses pictures and contrasts and stops short of an anatomy. It is a mistake to press the star-and-sun comparison, for instance, into a doctrine of fixed ranks of glory, since Paul's point there is that bodies come in different kinds and that God is able to provide the right one.

The command that follows from all this is clear: 'be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord,' verse 58. Hope in the resurrection is meant to make believers stable and productive, not to make them idle watchers of the sky.

Care is needed in reading verse 50, 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.' It describes the mortal condition of present human nature, not a rule that the future will contain no body. And the mystery of verses 51 and 52 describes an event, not a pattern to imitate. Speculation about timing and detail is not commended; Paul's own statement is that the mystery is told so that we know the outcome, which is victory.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by a spiritual body in verse 44?

views.label: A body animated and governed by the Spirit
views.case: The contrast is not matter versus non-matter but two animating principles: the natural body is enlivened by ordinary soul-life, the spiritual body is fully enlivened and ruled by the Holy Spirit, glorified and deathless yet truly a body, as the risen Christ shows.

views.label: An immaterial or ethereal body
views.case: Some have taken spiritual to mean non-physical, but this collides with the seed analogy of continuity and with the bodily resurrection of Christ, who ate and could be touched.

debates.bearing: The orthodox reading holds that the resurrection body is real and physical, transformed and Spirit-animated, not a ghostly or immaterial existence; the hope is a glorified body, not the loss of one.

debates.question: What does 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' mean in verse 50?

views.label: Mortal human nature as it now is
views.case: The second half of the verse says the same thing in other words: 'nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.' Flesh and blood therefore stands for humanity in its present, decaying condition, which must be changed before it can enter the age to come, verses 51 to 53.

views.label: Physical bodies are left behind
views.case: Some have read the verse as saying the material body has no place in the kingdom, and that only a soul or spirit enters. This is hard to reconcile with the context, where the raised dead are 'clothed' with imperishability, and with Luke 24:39, where the risen Jesus says, 'a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.'

debates.bearing: The passage contrasts the perishable with the imperishable, not the physical with the non-physical. The kingdom will be inhabited by bodies, raised and changed, and not by disembodied souls.

debates.question: Does Paul expect to be alive when Christ returns, 'we will not all sleep' in verse 51?

views.label: He includes himself as a possibility
views.case: Paul writes 'we' and speaks as one who hopes to be alive at the Lord's coming, as 1 Thessalonians 4:17 also suggests, while knowing he may die first, as 2 Corinthians 5:1 allows.

views.label: 'We' means believers in general
views.case: The 'we' is a way of speaking of the Christian company across time, divided into those who have died and those who have not, without any claim about Paul's own date.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands: whether a believer is asleep or alive at that day, all will be changed, and no one is left out.

study.originalLanguages:
The question 'with what kind of body?' leads to Paul's answer about 'natural' and 'spiritual.' The word 'natural' in verse 44 is psychikos, from psyche, soul or life. In 2:14 Paul used it of the person without the Spirit. It does not mean 'bad' or 'physical' but 'belonging to ordinary soul-life as we now have it.' The contrast is therefore between a body animated by the life we are born with and a body animated by the Spirit. The proof text in verse 45 uses the same root, since Genesis 2:7 says that the first man became a 'living being,' psyche zosa, in the Greek version, and the last Adam is a 'life-giving spirit.'

Verses 36 to 38 use a single, vivid picture, and one detail is worth seeing. The Greek of verse 37 speaks of a 'bare' grain, gymnon kokkon, so the seed is naked as well as small. Death, then, is a kind of undressing, and what comes up is clothed with a body that 'God has designed.' The objector is called aphron, 'senseless,' a sharp word for someone who has not thought the matter through.

In verses 40 to 41 the word for 'splendor' is doxa, glory, the same word translated 'glory' in verse 43. The heavenly bodies have doxa, and the sown body in dishonor is raised in doxa. Paul chooses a word that in the Septuagint belongs to God's own radiance, so the raised body shares in something of that.

In verse 47 the first man is 'of the dust,' from the Greek choikos, an adjective built on the word for earth and dust, and in verse 49 'likeness' translates eikon, image. Bearing the 'image' of the earthly man and the heavenly man recalls Genesis 1:26 to 27, where humanity is made in God's image, and Genesis 5:3, where Adam has a son in his own likeness. The verb for 'bear' is phoreo, to wear or carry like clothing, which leads naturally to verses 53 and 54.

Verse 51 calls the news a mysterion, a 'mystery.' In Paul this means something once hidden and now revealed, not something unknowable. The key verb is allasso, 'to change,' used twice in verses 51 and 52, 'we will all be changed.' The change is described with atomos, 'in an instant,' literally 'in what cannot be cut,' and rhipe ophthalmou, 'the twinkling of an eye.'

In verses 53 and 54 the verb is enduo, 'to put on' as a garment, so the perishable is dressed in the imperishable. In verse 54 death is 'swallowed up,' from katapino, to drink down or gulp, and the picture is of death itself being consumed. The 'sting' of verse 55 is kentron, a sharp point, used of a goad or a scorpion's sting. Death is a stinging creature that has lost its poison.

Finally, verse 58 uses two strong words for steadfast and immovable, hedraios and ametakinetos, 'firm as a seat' and 'not able to be moved.' The word for 'work' alongside is ergon, and 'labour,' kopos, means toil to exhaustion. The word for 'excel,' perisseuo, means to overflow or abound.

typology.type: The grain of wheat falling into the ground
typology.fulfillment: Jesus said, 'unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit,' John 12:24, and He said it about His own coming death. Paul turns the picture from Christ to Christ's people. The seed dies and is raised in a form that is continuous and yet new, and Christ's resurrection is the first fruit of the field that is His people. The escalation is that the harvest is not a field of grain but a company of persons who share His life. The type falls short in that a seed rises as a plant of its own kind, whereas believers rise in the likeness of another, the man from heaven.

typology.type: Dust and breath, and the breath that gives life
typology.fulfillment: In Genesis 2:7 God shaped the man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, and he became a living being. Paul reads that as the first stage of a two-stage story. The last Adam, as a life-giving spirit, does not merely receive life but gives it, as when the risen Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22. The correspondence is of dust and breath. The escalation is from a being who lives to a being who gives life. The type falls short in that Adam's life was lost by disobedience, while the Spirit's gift in Christ cannot be lost, for it carries the guarantee of resurrection, Romans 8:11.

typology.type: Bearing the image of a father
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 5:3 says that Adam 'had a son in his own likeness, after his own image.' The line of Adam passes on Adam's likeness, including his mortality, and the genealogy of that chapter ends each life with 'and then he died.' Paul says that we have borne the likeness of the man of dust and shall bear the likeness of the man from heaven, verse 49. Romans 8:29 says that those whom God foreknew He predestined 'to be conformed to the image of His Son.' The escalation is from a family likeness that ends in death to one that ends in glory. The type falls short because Seth inherited Adam's image by birth, while believers receive Christ's image by being united to Him.

In Israel, the trumpet marked great moments: the gathering at Sinai, Exodus 19:16, the call to assemble, Numbers 10:1 to 10, and the year of jubilee, when a trumpet sounded across the land and every person was to return to his property and his family, Leviticus 25:9 to 10. The jubilee trumpet was a liberation. Paul's last trumpet in verse 52 is the signal of the final release, when the dead are raised and the living changed. The correspondence is real as a pattern of proclamation and freedom. The type falls short in that the jubilee came every fifty years and was soon forgotten, while the last trumpet sounds once, and what it brings is permanent.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly by the title it gives Him in verses 45 to 49: the last Adam, the second man, the man from heaven. Each of the three says something. 'Last Adam' means that no one will come after Him to do what Adam failed to do, since He has done it. 'Second man' means He is truly human, standing in the line that began from the dust. 'From heaven' says that He is not merely the best of men but comes from God. In Him the two natures meet, and that is why He can bring the human race into a new kind of life.

He is a life-giving spirit. Adam received life, but Christ gives it. In John 5:21, 'just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes,' and in John 11:25 Jesus says, 'I am the resurrection and the life.' The Spirit of Christ who now lives in believers is the pledge of their future body, since 'He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit,' Romans 8:11. The believer's body is already a place where the future has begun.

He is the pattern of the body we will have. The risen Jesus is the only raised body we have seen. He could be touched, He ate fish, Luke 24:39 to 43, and bore the marks of the nails, John 20:27. Yet He passed into rooms with closed doors, John 20:19, and was not always at once recognised, Luke 24:16. The union of reality and mystery is the model for verses 42 to 44. Philippians 3:21 says it outright, that He 'will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body,' and 1 John 3:2 says, 'we will be like Him.'

He is the conqueror of death and sin. Death's sting is sin, verse 56, and Christ bore that sin, 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The law, which gave sin its power by revealing it, Romans 7:13, was satisfied in His death, Galatians 3:13. The victory of verse 57 is therefore 'through our Lord Jesus Christ,' since every step of the victory was His.

He is the one in whom labour has meaning. The closing words, 'in the Lord,' are not decoration. Work done in Christ is joined to the risen Lord, who will one day complete it, and Paul can say it is 'not in vain,' verse 58.

A caution is in order. The seed picture is Paul's own, drawn from nature, and while Jesus used a similar one, the details of the grain should not be treated as a code, as though the husk stood for the grave and the stalk for heaven. The picture supports a single idea: the dead are raised by God in a body of His own design, continuous with what was sown and yet far more glorious.
study.god:
The passage begins with God's generosity as a Creator. The seed, verse 38, is given 'a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body.' Behind a field of wheat stands a God who plans and provides. Paul's argument turns on the richness of creation: flesh of many kinds, bodies in heaven and on earth, stars that differ in splendor. A Creator that can make all of that is not stumped by the resurrection of one more kind of body.

He is a God who does not discard what He has made. The hope of the passage is that the same body that was buried is raised and changed, and not that it is replaced by a different one. This affirms that the material world and human bodies are good, as Genesis 1:31 said. Romans 8:21 says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay, and the same hope is held out for the body.

He is a God who transforms. 'We will all be changed,' verse 51. Change is not destruction. It is the work of one who takes the perishable and clothes it with the imperishable, who takes what is sown in weakness and raises it in power. His goal for His people is not a bare survival but glory.

He is the God who keeps His word. Paul closes with two prophets whose promises have lain unfulfilled for centuries, Isaiah and Hosea, and says that 'then the saying that is written will come to pass,' verse 54. God does not lose track of what He has said. Isaiah 25:8 spoke of God swallowing up death forever and wiping away tears from every face, and Paul sees that promise coming true.

He is the one from whom the triumph comes as a gift. The last verse reads, 'thanks be to God, who gives us the victory.' We do not take it by effort; it is handed to us, the Father's work in the Son, which is why the fitting response is thanks.

He is also a God who deals honestly with sin. Verse 56 says that 'the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.' Death is not a natural feature of a world God made, but the consequence of sin, and the law shows sin for what it is. The cure is not to pretend that death is gentle but to defeat the thing that makes it a sting. God's holiness and love meet in a victory that goes through the cross.

For worship the passage gives words: 'thanks be to God.' It also gives an ordinary way to show them, which is to stay at one's post. A God who has promised a harvest asks His people to keep sowing.

crossReferences.note: The source of Paul's 'living being' in verse 45. God shaped man from the dust and breathed life into him. Paul sets this first creation beside the last Adam, who is a life-giving spirit, and shows that the story that began with dust and breath is not abandoned but carried to a higher stage.

'He will swallow up death forever.' It stands in a vision of a feast for all nations where God wipes away tears. Paul's 'death has been swallowed up in victory' is his own rendering of this hope, and it declares that the long promise has reached its time.

'Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?' In Hosea the cry is set among threats of judgment, but it asks death a question and awaits an answer. Paul turns it into a taunt over a beaten enemy, since the day it was waiting for has come.

'Our lowly bodies' will be transformed 'to be like His glorious body,' by the same power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself. It is the plainest statement outside this chapter of what verse 49 means by bearing the likeness of the man from heaven.

The Lord descends with the trumpet of God, the dead in Christ rise first, and then the living are caught up to meet Him. It gives the sequence behind verses 51 and 52, with the trumpet, the rising, and the change of those still alive, and is written to comfort the grieving.

Jesus' saying about a kernel of wheat that must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit. It shows that the seed picture in verses 36 and 37 did not begin with Paul. Jesus Himself said that death is the path to fruitfulness, first for Himself and then for those who follow Him.

The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in believers and will give life to their mortal bodies. It joins Paul's 'spiritual body' to the Spirit's present work, and it makes the Spirit the link between Christ's rising and ours.

Believers 'groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.' The body is not to be abandoned but redeemed. The Spirit is the firstfruits, and the redemption of the body is the harvest that verses 42 to 44 describe.

The risen Jesus says, 'Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see.' The only resurrection body anyone has seen is solid and recognisable, which guards the phrase 'spiritual body' from being read as a ghost.

'We will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is.' John writes with the same hope as Paul in verse 49. What we shall be has not yet been revealed in full, but it is bound up with the sight of Christ and the likeness He gives.

Many who sleep in the dust will awake, and the wise will shine like the stars forever. It is the clearest Old Testament promise of a bodily rising, and it gives background to Paul's comparison of the glory of the stars in verses 40 to 42.

Paul speaks of an earthly tent dismantled and a building from God, of groaning to be clothed so that mortality may be swallowed up by life. It uses the same clothing language and the same word for swallowed up as verses 53 and 54, and shows how personal this hope was for him.

study.oneStory:
The question of this passage is where the whole Bible's story has been heading: what will become of the bodies that were made good, broken by sin, and laid in the ground? Genesis 1 made humanity out of the earth and called it very good. Genesis 3 pronounced the sentence that dust returns to dust. From then on, every grave in the Old Testament is a quiet witness that the sentence was carried out.

Within that story, the passage gives the final shape of redemption. Paul says that the story has two Adams and two bodies. The first man brought the natural body, which is sown in weakness and ends in the dust. The last Adam gives the spiritual body, raised in power. The order matters, 'not first the spiritual, but the natural, and then the spiritual,' verse 46, and it is the order of the whole plot: creation, fall, redemption and new creation. The passage does not leave redemption as a rescue of souls but extends it to bodies, so that what was lost in Eden is not just restored but exceeded.

The passage looks back. The pictures of the seed and the many kinds of flesh recall the creation account, with its 'each according to its kind,' and the 'living being' of Genesis 2:7. The clothing of the perishable with the imperishable answers the clothing God gave Adam and Eve after the fall, Genesis 3:21, and the nakedness that was the first mark of shame. Death's sting, sin, traces to the same garden.

It also looks forward. Verse 52's trumpet and verse 54's swallowing up of death carry into Revelation, where 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. Romans 8:21 says that creation itself will be set free, and Paul's word for the harvest of bodies belongs with the renewal of the heavens and the earth. The tree of life, withheld in Genesis 3:24, is open again in Revelation 22:2.

Between the two ends lies the present, and the passage ends there: 'Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable.' The labour of the church, its preaching, its care for the poor, its patient faithfulness, is the labour of people who have seen the end of the story. They are not building for a world that will be lost, but sowing in a field whose harvest has been promised by the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

quiz.q: What does the seed analogy teach about the resurrection body?

options.text: The body is both continuous with this one and gloriously transformed, as a plant is related to its seed.
options.note: Sown perishable, raised imperishable: continuity and transformation together.

options.text: The old body is discarded and a completely unrelated one appears.
options.note: The seed image stresses continuity, not a wholly unrelated body.

options.text: There is no body at all, only a soul.
options.note: Paul insists the resurrection is bodily, sown and raised.

options.text: The resurrection body is the very same body, essentially unchanged.
options.note: Right that it is the same body, but it is gloriously transformed, not unchanged.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by a spiritual body?

options.text: A real body fully animated and governed by the Holy Spirit, glorified and deathless.
options.note: Spiritual describes the animating power, not an immaterial substance.

options.text: A ghostly, immaterial existence with no body.
options.note: That contradicts the bodily resurrection of Christ and the seed analogy.

options.text: A radiant, glorified body unlike the present one in every way.
options.note: Close: it is glorious and transformed, yet it remains continuous with this body, as the seed shows.

options.text: The same weak, perishable body we have now.
options.note: It is raised imperishable and powerful, not left weak and perishable.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the last Adam?

options.text: A life-giving spirit and the man from heaven, whose image we will bear.
options.note: Christ gives resurrection life and remakes us in His heavenly likeness.

options.text: The first man, formed from the dust of the earth.
options.note: That is the first Adam; Christ is the last Adam from heaven.

options.text: The risen Christ who shares resurrection life as all believers will.
options.note: He is risen, but more than a fellow recipient: He is a life-giving spirit who bestows resurrection life.

options.text: An angel who never took a body.
options.note: He is the man from heaven, truly human and risen bodily.

quiz.q: What happens to death according to verses 54 to 57?

options.text: It is swallowed up in victory, its sting drawn, and the victory is given us through Christ.
options.note: Death is defeated, and the victory is God's gift through our Lord Jesus Christ.

options.text: Death remains undefeated and always wins.
options.note: Paul proclaims death swallowed up in victory.

options.text: Death is defeated, and we share in that defeat by our own effort.
options.note: Right that death is truly defeated, but the victory is God's gift through Christ, not our achievement.

options.text: Death is merely ignored, not truly conquered.
options.note: It is genuinely conquered, swallowed up in victory.

quiz.q: What practical charge closes the chapter in verse 58?

options.text: Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the Lord's work, for your labor is not in vain.
options.note: The certainty of resurrection grounds steadfast, hopeful labor.

options.text: Withdraw from the world and wait passively for the end.
options.note: Paul calls for active, abounding work, not passivity.

options.text: Live for pleasure since the future is secure.
options.note: The call is to excel in the Lord's work, not to indulge.

options.text: Rest in the finished victory, since our effort now adds nothing.
options.note: The victory is indeed finished in Christ, yet Paul calls us to abound in the Lord's work, for it is not in vain.

questions: Paul insists the resurrection is of the body, not merely the soul. How does the hope of a glorified body change the way you view your physical life now?
The resurrection body is this body transformed, sown in weakness and raised in power. Where do you long for the day when what is perishable is clothed with the imperishable?
We will bear the image of the man from heaven, Christ Himself. How does the promise of becoming like Him shape who you are becoming today?
Death is swallowed up in victory, and the victory is a gift through Christ. How does that free you from the fear of death?
Because your labor in the Lord is not in vain, Paul says to be steadfast and immovable. What work for the Lord do you need to keep at, trusting it matters forever?

translationNotes.note: A spiritual body does not mean immaterial; the word describes a body animated and governed by the Holy Spirit, glorified and deathless, in contrast to the natural body enlivened by ordinary soul-life.

The first line quotes Genesis 2:7, the first man Adam became a living being; Paul caps it with his own inspired addition, the last Adam a life-giving spirit, drawing the contrast between the two heads of humanity.
Death has been swallowed up in victory draws on Isaiah 25:8, and the taunt where, O Death, is your sting echoes Hosea 13:14; Paul weaves both prophecies into his announcement of death's defeat.
